content: A plaster mold or a computer-generated digital image is often utilized in the fabrication of prosthetic or orthotic devices. The fabrication process typically involves shaping and assembling various components and materials, many of which are pre-manufactured and available in different models and sizes. While some devices can be fabricated while the user waits, a fully customized device usually requires a separate appointment. Prosthetics and orthotics professionals must adhere strictly to the manufacturer’s instructions and guidelines to ensure the proper use of components and to minimize risks to both users and personnel. Any deviations from standard practices must be thoroughly documented. Manufacturers and suppliers of prosthetic and orthotic components, materials, and consumables are responsible for informing and training personnel on the optimal clinical application of their products. Once the device is fabricated, it is fitted to the user and adjusted to align with the body’s anatomical features and movement patterns. Individual customization is essential to achieve optimal comfort, functionality, and appearance, ensuring the device can be used effectively. This customization process often occurs alongside user training. Depending on the complexity of the device, customization may be immediate for prefabricated products or may require multiple sessions, taking days, weeks, or even months in exceptional cases. User training is a critical component of prosthetics and orthotics service delivery. Many users require preparatory training to strengthen muscles and increase joint mobility before being fitted with a prosthesis or orthosis. During the fitting process, users must receive sufficient functional training to become accustomed to the device, learn how to don and doff it, use it safely and effectively, and control its features and functions. Training is typically supervised by a prosthetics and orthotics clinician, physiotherapist, or occupational therapist. Adjustments to the device may be made as needed based on the user’s progress. Users generally require less training when renewing a prosthesis or orthosis. For those needing regular support in daily activities, family members and caregivers should be involved in all training steps. Physiotherapy and occupational therapy interventions are often necessary during preparatory training and the fitting phase, particularly for first-time users. These interventions may include strengthening muscles and joints through supervised exercises, massage, and occasionally electrotherapy or heat treatments. Functional training begins during the initial trials with the device to optimize fit and function. This training includes guiding users in movement, supervising gait training, and supporting functional activities to ensure the device can be effectively integrated into daily life. Therapy is integral to the overall treatment outcome and should ideally be part of the prosthetics and orthotics service unit, though therapists are often external resources. Once the prosthesis or orthosis is deemed optimal in fit, function, and comfort, and the user is confident in its use, the responsible clinician must conduct a final thorough check of all features before delivery. Users and caregivers should have the final say on the device’s acceptability. At delivery, the clinician should review all essential treatment criteria with the user and caregivers, ensuring they understand how to use and maintain the device, when to return for follow-up, and where to go for maintenance and repair. Users are responsible for adhering to these instructions, and a follow-up appointment should be scheduled before they leave the service unit. The outcomes of treatment should be evaluated during product delivery and follow-up sessions against the agreed treatment goals using validated outcome measures. This evaluation should document technical results, improvements in the user’s functioning, mobility, dexterity, and activity, as well as the impact on participation in work, education, social inclusion, and quality of life. Follow-up appointments should be individualized based on the intervention type and user’s age, with children requiring at least biannual follow-ups. These sessions verify the product’s usefulness, address any issues with fit, comfort, or function, and provide necessary maintenance and repairs. Follow-up is as critical as any other step in the delivery process and offers an opportunity to collect data for quality assurance and service improvement. Maintenance and repair services must be available to extend the lifespan of prostheses and orthoses. These services can be provided by the service unit or collaborating units. Effective management of a prosthetics and orthotics service unit involves planning, monitoring, financial management, stock management, material procurement, human resources management, data management, and quality assurance. Planning should include long-term and annual strategic and operational plans with clear aims, benchmarks, and performance indicators to facilitate monitoring and evaluation. Monitoring involves regular data collection and analysis to ensure activities progress as planned, while evaluation, often conducted by external specialists, assesses the relevance, effectiveness, efficiency, and impact of the unit’s activities. Collaboration with stakeholders, such as user groups, health and rehabilitation services, and local government, is essential. Formalized working relationships, regular meetings, and advisory committees can enhance service planning and delivery. Financial management should ensure the service has a solid foundation, can grow sustainably, and has a long-term impact. Transparency and adherence to standard practices are crucial. Stock management and material procurement should be carefully planned to ensure cost-effectiveness and uninterrupted service delivery. Human resources management should follow established procedures, including workforce planning, recruitment, staff satisfaction, and retention. Annual performance appraisals should compare individual employee productivity against agreed objectives. Data management is vital for planning, budgeting, monitoring, and evaluating services. Consistent data collection and analysis provide insights into service success and help identify areas for improvement. Anonymized data should be sent to central levels for national analysis. Integrated computerized systems and electronic clinical records can facilitate effective data management and reporting. Quality management ensures that products and treatments meet established requirements. A quality assurance system should measure, monitor, and improve the quality of products and services, addressing both technical quality and user satisfaction. This process corresponds to a clinical audit of healthcare services.
